prompt.context: Our client 'V-Formulae' is a baby food formula producer. The client's main ingredient in most of the products it sells is milk. The client has machinery that pasteurizes the milk and evaporates it to create a powder, which is then used in most V-Formulae products available in the market. The client is US-based and all of its sales are only in the US. V-Formulae is the market leader; however there are two other major competitors with significant market share. There are numerous smaller players but they do not have more than 10% of the market. The client's profits have declined over the last three quarters, and the client suspects that the cost of milk is affecting the margins.
prompt.question: A supplier has approached our client and offered a five-year fixed contract to supply milk at 10% below the current market price. We need to help our client figure out whether they should enter into this contract with the supplier.

clarifying_info.q: What type of milk does V-Formulae currently source?
clarifying_info.a: The company sources only cow's milk today.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other major cost drivers besides milk?
clarifying_info.a: Milk is the primary ingredient and the main cost concern; the case focuses on milk pricing.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market price of milk?
clarifying_info.a: The current market price is $18 per unit (2012 figure from Exhibit 1).

clarifying_info.q: What is the contract offer price?
clarifying_info.a: The five-year fixed contract price is $16.20 per unit, which is 10% below the current market price of $18.

clarifying_info.q: Can V-Formulae raise the price of its end products?
clarifying_info.a: The average product selling price has more or less remained stable, indicating the market is price-elastic and V-Formulae does not have a lot of leeway to increase prices.

exhibits.title: Milk Price vs. Average Product Selling Price (2008–2012)
exhibits.shows: A dual-line chart and accompanying table showing the annual milk price and the average product selling price from 2008 to 2012.

exhibits.title: Historical Milk Prices (long-run trend)
exhibits.shows: A time-series chart showing the long-run historical price of milk, including levels before and after 2005.

data.key_observation: Milk prices crossed historical highs in 2005 and have been rising continuously since then.

exhibits.title: Historical Price of Corn per Bushel
exhibits.shows: A time-series chart showing the historical price of corn per bushel, with values ranging from 0 to approximately 12.

data.key_observation: Corn prices rose sharply around 2008 and remained elevated.

framework: Understand current cost structure and margin pressure — review milk cost as % of COGS and profitability trend
Analyze milk price history and future outlook — is the current high price structural or cyclical?
Assess supply-side drivers of milk price — livestock feed costs (corn), farmland, herd size, output per cow
Assess demand-side drivers — emerging market demand, domestic consumption growth
Evaluate sourcing alternatives — different milk types (goat, soy), different geographies, backward integration
Evaluate the contract terms — price (10% discount), duration (5 years), lock-in risk vs. certainty benefit
Competitive dynamics — risk that competitors sign the contract if V-Formulae declines
Recommendation — enter contract or not, and on what terms

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What does the data tell you about the profitability situation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Milk price rose from $14 to $18 (2008–2012), a 28.5% increase over five years. Average product selling price rose only from $21 to $22.50, a ~7% increase. The gap between selling price and milk cost is compressing, which directly explains the margin decline. The market appears price-elastic — V-Formulae cannot easily pass cost increases on to consumers.

steps: = 28.5% increase in milk price over five years

questions.prompt: What are the major reasons for the sustained increase in milk prices?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers both supply and demand sides: Demand — rising demand from emerging economies (China, India) for dairy; domestic consumption trends. Supply — corn is the major livestock feed; corn prices rose sharply after a US government mandate in 2008 required corn to be used for ethanol production, raising feed costs and thus milk production costs; decreasing farmland reduces herd sizes; output per cow may be declining due to health or nutrition issues.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows long-run historical milk prices. What hypothesis does this support?
questions.guidance: Milk prices crossed historical highs around 2005 and have been rising ever since — the recent price level is not a temporary spike but a persistent structural shift. A strong candidate connects this to global demand growth in emerging economies as a structural driver, distinct from the cyclical corn-price factor.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 3 shows corn prices per bushel. What does this tell you about the milk price outlook?
questions.guidance: Corn is the major livestock feed. The sharp rise in corn prices (driven by the 2008 US government mandate to use corn for ethanol) is the primary cause of rising milk production costs. Critically, the government mandate expires in 2012 — corn prices are therefore expected to fall, which should reduce livestock feed costs and in turn put downward pressure on milk prices. This is the key insight that tips the decision against signing a long 5-year fixed contract at today's elevated price.

questions.prompt: Should V-Formulae sign the five-year fixed milk supply contract at $16.20 (10% below current market price of $18)?
questions.guidance: Strong answer synthesizes the exhibits: The contract price of $16.20 looks attractive today, but the corn mandate expiry in 2012 is expected to lower feed costs and therefore milk prices. A five-year lock-in at $16.20 could leave V-Formulae paying above-market prices once milk prices fall. The risk of locking in is high over a five-year horizon. A shorter 1–2 year contract would capture the near-term discount while avoiding long-run lock-in risk. Competitive risk: if V-Formulae declines, competitors may sign, giving them a cost advantage.

math.setup: Contract offer price = current market price × (1 - 0.10)
math.answer: Contract price = $16.20/unit (10% below current $18 market price)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the major reasons the price of milk has increased over the past five years?

categories.name: Demand-side factors
ideas: Rising dairy demand in emerging economies (China, India)
Growing middle class increasing protein/dairy consumption globally

categories.name: Supply-side factors
ideas: Government mandate (2008) requiring corn to be used for ethanol raised livestock feed costs
Decrease in farmland and therefore fewer cows producing milk
Declining output per cow due to health issues or nutrition
Drought and extreme weather reducing livestock sustainability
Higher veterinary and livestock maintenance costs

categories.name: Market structure
ideas: Milk is a commodity — prices are market-determined, not firm-controlled
Limited short-run supply elasticity for dairy (herd size cannot change quickly)
Consolidation among dairy producers reducing competitive pressure on price

categories.name: Sourcing and alternatives
ideas: Explore goat milk or soy-based alternatives if nutritional profile is equivalent
Consider importing milk from lower-cost producing regions
Evaluate backward integration into milk production to control cost

recommendation: Do NOT sign the five-year fixed contract at $16.20 — the corn mandate expires in 2012 and milk prices are expected to decline, making a five-year lock-in at current elevated prices unattractive
If any contract is signed, negotiate a shorter 1–2 year term to capture the current 10% discount without long-run lock-in risk
risks: If milk prices do not fall (e.g., demand from emerging markets remains strong), declining the contract leaves V-Formulae exposed to continued price increases
Competitors may sign the contract and gain a sustained cost advantage
A shorter contract may not be available on equivalent discount terms
next_steps: Negotiate a 1–2 year contract rather than the full five-year term
Work closely with milk farms to understand cost structures and explore alternative feeds (e.g., soybean) to reduce their costs and potentially pass savings through
Evaluate alternate milk sources (goat milk) for nutrient equivalency and regulatory compliance
Monitor corn price trajectory post-mandate expiry to time any future contract negotiations
